coverage: Covering roughly Nov 22–23, 2026. Compiled Monday, ET.

items.headline: Alexandr Wang: "Superintelligence is arriving," and the path is not inevitable
items.summary: Meta's chief AI officer published an X Article arguing that the Riemann Hypothesis proof marks the start of a real change: the gaps left for models are no longer intelligence but know-how, plumbing and experimentation, and AI research itself is easier than that proof, so models will likely be able to automate it. It drew the biggest response in his feed overnight. After critics quoted his line that it is hard to imagine humanity keeping control over unconstrained recursive self-improvement, he followed up that "this path is not inevitable," pointing to Meta delaying Muse for months, the SI Accords, and Mark Zuckerberg's call for labs to spend most compute serving customers rather than on self-improvement.
items.short: The essay that dominated the feed; read it as one lab leader's view.

items.headline: Trump says he hopes Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang; Arm's Rene Haas stays put
items.summary: President Trump said he hopes Nvidia's board rehires Jensen Huang, after Treasury Secretary Bessent said on Sunday that Nvidia should look outside for a leader and "he's on the outside now," and that he is not worried about circular financing given "near unlimited demand" for its chips. Then Arm CEO Rene Haas, widely seen as a leading candidate for the Nvidia job, was named SoftBank's Vice Chairman from Dec. 1 and reaffirmed his "long-term commitment" to Arm. @KobeissiLetter reported Nvidia up more than 8% premarket. @GavinSBaker: "Odds going up every day imo."
items.short: Washington openly backs Jensen's return; the obvious outside candidate takes himself out.

items.headline: Nasdaq 100 futures jump nearly 4% as dip buyers return to chips
items.summary: After the worst week for tech in decades, @KobeissiLetter reported Nasdaq 100 futures up nearly 4% before the open, which would be the index's biggest daily gain since May 2025, led by chip stocks. @oguzerkan wrote that there isn't much room left on the downside "unless we get an unexpected systemic shock." Goldman data shared by @ParadisLabs over the weekend showed the heaviest weekly shorting of U.S. stocks since June 2022.
items.short: A premarket bounce, not yet a trading day; futures can fade.

items.headline: GLM-5.4 brings the "loop transformer" to an open lab
items.summary: The GLM team introduced GLM-5.4, its first Loop Transformer: it loops existing layers of the GLM-5 base model for deeper reasoning and extends coding to video, games, 3D shaders and CAD, with API access after a safety evaluation and weights to be "released responsibly." @zephyr_z9 expects more "loopers" in the next three to four months and an Astra 6-like jump for open labs once they scale to 2-3 trillion parameters.
items.short: Looping, the trick behind this fall's big closed-model jumps, reaches open models.

Most people use AI to speed up the tasks they already do. Shopify CEO @tobi says the real skill is learning to play it:  

“I think AI is best thought of as an instrument.”  

“If you first pick up a guitar, you can maybe figure out how to play a melody or something, but you don't really know how to produce music. It takes a while.”  

“There's no difference between the guitar you can pick up and what Hendrix plays.”  

"There's a small group of people in the world who can play AI at this [Hendrix] level who are really understanding the tools, even though it's a very fast moving base."

"And I think I'm reporting back a little bit from what the world looks like from that perspective. Instead of accelerating your tasks, learn the instrument, learn how to work with AI in such a way that you provide it with the problems you want to solve. Show up with an openness for a wide variety of solutions because it turns out there often are things that you might never have thought of."

"Almost all engineering at Shopify now runs through factories: constellations of AI agents with different jobs that collaborate and accomplish long horizon tasks."  

“It's much better to be more ambitious with AI and have it do reps on solving the problem than it is to accomplish tasks.”

items.author: Daniel
items.text:
$CBRS x $AMD is coming to Cerebras Inference Cloud and its partners’ infrastructure by the end of 2027.

AI inference has two stages:

• Prefill: Processing the prompt.
• Decode: Generating the response.

GPUs are extremely good at the first.

But when it comes to generating tokens at extreme speed, Cerebras is built for exactly that job.

AMD Instinct GPUs handle prefill, while Cerebras CS-3 systems handle decode.

By offloading prompt processing to GPUs, Cerebras can dedicate its systems entirely to generating tokens.

The result is 5x more token throughput per megawatt compared to a CS-3-only configuration, without sacrificing generation speed.

Cerebras plans to deploy this architecture across hundreds of megawatts by the end of 2027.

The demand for ultrafast inference is exploding, and Cerebras is proving that its technology can complement the world’s leading AI accelerators rather than compete against them.

Cerebras doesn’t need to replace GPUs. It can work alongside them.

And AMD is far from the only major player Cerebras is working with.

• $AMZN: Bringing Cerebras chips to AWS alongside Trainium.

• $MSFT: Partnering with Cerebras to accelerate AI inference.

• $ORCL: Bringing ultrafast inference to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure.

Cerebras is positioning itself to become the token-generation layer across the entire AI cloud ecosystem, regardless of which chips power the prefill stage.

items.text:
People love the idea that AI/SI will dominate the world, and the stock market must keep going up...

I have a contrarian point of view. The internet was heralded as the most important infrastructure, most of us can't live w/o it today. Global commerce, finance, information, and communications flourished.  I would argue it was as important as AI/SI for its time. 

My friend works at CableOne, a cable internet company, and he asked me whether he should buy it now it's cheaper. Peaked at $2000, back down to $2. I looked at the books, 1.6B revenue, -$400m operating loss. 2Bil debt.   Internet is great but, infra is expensive, low margin because customers want cheap data, very competitive (not good for the top line and margin, high capex => high debt, low margin).

We love the internet, but not low margin infra like this.

items.author: Pepe Invests
items.text:
I'm considering selling everything this week.

Every single share.

I've been thinking about this for months, and if you've been following me, you know how much I've talked about it.

The only reason I didn't sell sooner is that I deviated from my plan.

I got greedy and used the cash reserves I had been building to buy companies I believed were at a discount.

In my eyes, it's time to revisit my original plan.

I feel very uneasy about the world we're heading into.

If you've been paying attention the past few weeks, something big has been happening.

A national flight ground stop, the longest since 9/11.

Major banks failing to process transfers.

Microsoft, Apple, and government networks going down.

Officials are calling these separate technical failures.

In my opinion, I don't buy that. 

I believe we are under large scale cyber attacks.

So think about what happens if the stock market itself gets hit.

Not just one exchange, but trading halts, brokerage platforms freezing, or the systems that settle trades going down.

Something tells me it would look like a bank run, where everyone tries to get out at once and nobody can.

And that would only be the small version of this.

If a more critical national system gets hit and goes out, how much do people panic?

I'm not trying to scare you. 

This is simply how I see the reality we're living in.

I also have significant realized gains that I can offset with my current losses, which makes the timing make sense.

Most accounts would sell without saying anything because they fear the backlash.

I'd rather be open with you, because I've always been transparent about my logic and decision making, right or wrong.

Right now I'm going off intuition, and I don't care what anyone thinks about that.

These next few days will be pivotal for my investing journey, for better or for worse.

I'll make my decision by Tuesday.

This is not meant for anyone to follow or to worry you.

It's simply me being transparent about how I'm thinking.

In my opinion, getting back to my original plan matters more than staying fully invested in a market I feel uneasy about.

Worth rereading a month later against this week's MW announcements, and as a reminder that it is one bull's model, not guidance.

items.title: The agent that built a robot's training course on stage
items.author: Nous Research
items.summary: Nous describes Jensen Huang's GTC Berlin finale: he set up a customized Hermes agent in one prompt, then had it plan an obstacle course, have another model build it with FreeCAD, Blender and Isaac Lab, and train thousands of simulated Hugging Face Microducks until a policy was ready for the real robot. A concrete picture of chained local and cloud models doing real work, and a timely reminder of what Jensen was building weeks before he left.

items.title: Four Cards
items.rule: If a parcel is marked Express, it has a red sticker.
items.explanation: Express could hide something that breaks the rule; Blue sticker breaks it if the other side turns out to be Express. Red sticker can't break it (the rule never says only those cards have it), and Standard isn't covered by the rule at all. Most people pick the card that matches the rule's second half instead of the one that could falsify it.
